name: I'M GUACING HERE BURGER (Comes with Guacamole)

recipe.history:
The avocado tree is a native of the tropical highlands of south-central Mexico and Guatemala, where wild Persea drymifolia and Persea americana have grown for millions of years. Archaeological evidence from the Tehuacan Valley in Puebla, Mexico, places human use of wild avocados at approximately 10,000 BCE, and deliberate cultivation appears to have begun around 5,000 BCE, making it one of the earliest domesticated fruits of the Western Hemisphere. The Aztec and Mayan civilizations integrated the avocado into their economies, cosmologies, and cuisines deeply; the Aztec calendar featured a day named after the ahuacatl, and the fruit was traded as currency in some regions. Guacamole — from the Nahuatl words ahuacatl and molli, meaning avocado sauce — was prepared in stone mortars called molcajetes, using only avocado, tomato, and chili at its most ancient, and later evolving to include onion, lime, cilantro, and garlic as Spanish ingredients mingled with indigenous ones in post-conquest Mexican kitchens.

The avocado's arrival in the American mainstream was a gradual process shaped by California agriculture. The Hass avocado, which now dominates global markets, was discovered as a chance seedling by Rudolph Hass, a mail carrier in La Habra Heights, California, in the 1920s. Its creamy texture, high fat content, and superior shelf life compared to other varieties made it the ideal commercial avocado, and California's avocado groves became the engine of the American guacamole market. By the 1980s, guacamole had become the signature condiment of Tex-Mex and Californian cuisine, appearing on virtually every Mexican-American restaurant menu in the country. The chunky, thick-style guacamole — where avocado is mashed only partially, leaving substantial pieces intact — became the premium form, distinguished from the smoother, thinner dips by its texture, freshness, and the sense that it was made to order.

I have a specific memory of the first time I understood that guacamole was a living thing, not a jar. I was twenty-three, at a restaurant where they made it tableside in a molcajete, and the server let me choose the heat level and the amount of lime. She seasoned it at the table and pushed it across. I could see the avocado still had its grain, the tomato was barely mixed in, the cilantro was in whole leaves. It was incomparably better than anything I had eaten from a container. I went home and never bought guacamole in a jar again. The thick, chunky guacamole on this burger is made the same way — handled lightly, seasoned boldly, assembled at the last possible moment.

A burger topped with thick, chunky guacamole must be cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center. The guacamole is cold, creamy, acidic with lime, and rich with avocado fat. It is a generous, assertive topping. The beef beneath it must be equally assertive — warm, juicy, with a thick caramelized crust that provides bitter contrast to the creamy green above. Medium rare is the only doneness that achieves this balance. The fat in the avocado and the fat in the beef communicate with each other in a medium-rare burger in a way they never can in a well-done one. This is not metaphor. It is food chemistry and it is the reason this burger works.
ingredients: 1/2 cup sharp cheddar cheese, finely shredded
1 fresh jalapeño, seeded and finely minced
1/3 cup white onion, very finely diced
2 Roma tomatoes, cored, seeded, and cut into 1/4-inch dice
Salt and white pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Make the jalapeño cheddar buns: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water; bloom 10 minutes. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture and softened butter; knead on medium 5 minutes. Add shredded cheddar and minced jalapeño; knead 3–4 more minutes until incorporated.

2. Cover and rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 125g each). Shape into tight rounds, place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with extra shredded cheddar. Proof 45 minutes. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 20–22 minutes until golden and cheese on top is lightly crisped. Cool on rack.
3. Make the sour cream sauce: Whisk all ingredients together, adjust seasoning. Refrigerate.

4. Make the chunky guacamole: Halve and pit avocados. Score the flesh in a crosshatch pattern with a knife, making 1/2-inch cubes, then scoop into a bowl. Add lime juice and salt immediately; fold gently once. Add jalapeño, white onion, tomato, cilantro, garlic, cumin, and cayenne. Fold together with a fork, leaving substantial chunks of avocado intact. Taste and adjust lime and salt. The texture should be thick, chunky, and deeply textured — not smooth. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface and refrigerate until assembly. Prepare no more than 45 minutes before serving.

5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties slightly wider than the buns. Press a center dimple. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and cumin.
6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil.

7. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until a deep, even crust forms. Flip once. Place a slice of Monterey Jack on each. Cook 2–3 more minutes, tenting to melt cheese, until an instant-read thermometer inserted in the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
8. Split jalapeño cheddar buns and toast cut-side down in the skillet fat 60–90 seconds.
9. Assemble: Spread sour cream sauce on both cut faces of each bun. Place shredded romaine on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice and red onion rings; season tomato with flaky salt.

10. Place the Monterey Jack-topped patty on top. Using a large spoon, pile a thick, generous mound of chunky guacamole onto the patty — this is a comes-with-guacamole burger, so do not restrain yourself. The guacamole should form a visible mound above the level of the bun.
11. Season the guacamole with a pinch of flaky salt and a squeeze of lime. Add hot sauce if desired. Crown with the top bun, press gently, and serve with lime wedges immediately.
